Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.

Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

# Seller Analysis: Project Kestrel — Departures from Buyer Playbook

## 1. Aggregate General Warranty Cap (Clause 12.1)
**Playbook:** General cap at **25% / AUD 6,000,000** (starting position); a 20% / AUD 4,800,000 cap is only acceptable with Amelia Frost prior written authority identifying the draft. That authority has not been given.

**Seller position:** 20% / AUD 4,800,000 — unconditional.

**Analysis:** This is the single largest structural departure. Reducing the general cap below the baseline leaves no cushion for known or latent items under DD-003 to DD-012, especially Riverlark (~AUD 3.2M, possibly unaudited), Export/privacy (unconfirmed), Employee bonuses (AUD 420K unitemised), and Sandbar renewals (AUD 330K). Under your playbook a lower cap is only removable with buyer-principal authorisation, which has not occurred. Leaving it in would forfeit the negotiated starting position without any offsetting goodwill concession elsewhere.

**Push back:** Accept the 20% / AUD 4,800,000 cap only with a written amendment clause referencing the Seller Update 2026 draft by Appendix Date, identifying the authority, naming the seller’s counsel and seller principal authorisation letter. Without that, the draft risk falls entirely on buyer. Alternatively, return the Seller Update mark-up and insist on the 25% starting cap.

---

## 2. Thresholds — De minimis and Basket (Clause 12.2)
**Playbook:** de minimis AUD 5,000; aggregate basket AUD 50,000, seller liable from the first dollar once exceeded.

**Seller position:** de minimis AUD 25,000; basket AUD 250,000.

**Analysis:** Both thresholds are inflated in the seller’s favour by a factor of ten. At AUD 25,000 minimum there is effectively no protection for small but real operational incidents such as the Export matter (DD-006 ~1,240 records), supplier renewals timing or office-lease terminology. At AUD 250,000 basket, cumulative small claims can accumulate below any meaningful benchmark before any recovery kicks in.

**Push back:** Revert both thresholds to the playbook values (AUD 5,000 / AUD 50,000). If either is contested, require proof of the adjusted figure plus Amelia Frost approval, but absent that, impose the playbook standard.

---

## 3. Time Limits (Clause 12.3 / 13)
**Playbook:** General claims period 24 months post-Completion; 18 months is a fallback requiring Amelia Frost written approval (none given).

**Seller position:** 18 months, with the “applies to all Claims” broad catch-all language.

**Analysis:** The seller has committed to the reduced time window without any fallback mechanism, effectively locking out claims for 18 months on a broad interpretation of “Claims”. The broad “applies to all Claims” wording could also swallow Fundamental/Title claims, which your playbook keeps outside the general basket/de minimis bars. That matters because title defects discovered later often involve latent fraud or concealed incapacity.

**Push back:** Restore the 24-month general period. If the seller wants shortened for specific Category A items, propose 18 months only with enhanced disclosure support (case-by-case exhibits), not a blanket extension. Keep Fundamental/Title claims on the 24-month general regime at least with an appropriate knowledge bar. Do not allow the broad “applies to all Claims” language to extend beyond fundamental claims without explicit fund wagering.

---

## 4. Capacity & Title under Same Cap (Fundamental/Title Restructuring)
**Playbook:** Separate regime, 100% cap, at least six years, outside the general basket/de minimis/knowledge bar.

**Seller position:** Capacity and title warranties subject to same caps and time limits as general warranties.

**Analysis:** This conflates two distinct warranty categories. Title issues frequently involve concealment or incapacity that should benefit from the longer six-year window and the 100% hard cap. The seller’s reclassification removes those protections the buyer negotiated, so cap and period carry over into the more exposed category, compounding our loss across multiple categories instead of protecting them independently.

**Push back:** Restore the separate regime. Title claims must be capped at 100%, generally open-ended from Completion (or at least five years, depending on jurisdiction), and excluded from the general thresholds. Maintain independence between Title/Capacity and general warranties.

---

## 5. Limitations, Exclusive Remedies & Non-Reliance (Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5)
**Playbook:** Fraud, wilful concealment and deliberate misconduct carved out to the maximum extent enforceable; no one may waive this carve-out.

**Seller position:** Limitations, exclusive remedies and non-reliance apply to all Claims of any nature, with no carve-out stated.

**Analysis:** With no fraud carve-out, any confidential breach or mis-representation discovered post-Completion cannot be recovered unless it survives every limitation shield. That is dangerous in connection with employee bonus timing (DD-005), Export scope and possible buyer knowledge gaps. In short, the seller assumes all caps operate without exception, including against seller-perceived excluded conduct.

**Push back:** Add an express fraud carve-out mirroring the buyer’s policy. State that in no event do limitations, baskets, caps, exclusive remedies or non-reliance bar recovery for fraud, wilful concealment, deliberate misconduct or similar seller-fault conduct. Any attempted waiver must be struck as unreasonable.

---

## 6. Disclosure Standards
**Playbook:** Specific fair disclosure; reject whole-data-room, public-register or prudent-search deemed disclosure.

**Seller position:** General disclosure of data room and public registers, Schedule 7 relies on that.

**Analysis:** The seller offers no specific, itemised disclosure about the flagged items: DD-005 bonuses taxed/on-cost status; DD-006 breach confirmation, notification duty, harm or loss amount; DD-008 timing/scope per renewal; DD-010 bank verification status; DD-012 buyer self-verification. The “general disclosure” wording also risks being imprecise for obligations that need case-specific documentation.

**Push back:** Require itemised disclosure for each material item:

- DD-005: state payroll tax, superannuation and on-cost treatment.
- DD-006: establish whether breach is confirmed, whether notification duty exists, quantified harm/loss, remediation steps.
- DD-008: specify each renewal’s temporal relationship and ordinary-course characterisation.
- DD-010: state that this is seller’s internal source, request independent bank verification, flag any gap.
- DD-012: affirm Buyer completed independent verification of ownership, not reliance solely on register.

Treat general data-room disclosure as illustrative only; require the Schedule 7 entries to be substantiated by specific exhibits.

---

## 7. Bluefen Consent
**Playbook:** Effective consent AND evidence that conditions are satisfied, before Completion; reasonable endeavours alone insufficient.

**Seller position:** Consent treated as satisfied on delivery; conditions in clauses 11.2/11.3 assumed satisfied.

**Analysis:** The disclosure confirms no final written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied as at letter date. Providing that in the SPA closes the window with no supporting record, which invites dispute about whether consent was effective pre-Completion or post-Completion. Buyer may be left relying on a deemed consent while seller has ultimate knowledge of conditions.

**Push back:** Insert a condition precedent: effective written consent of Bluefen plus evidence that all associated change-control conditions are satisfied, delivered before Completion. Treat the current draft as incomplete.

---

## 8. Riverlank Release Mechanism
**Playbook:** Current payout + direct repayment from Completion funds + effective security releases; a post-completion release needs irrevocable undertaking + Amelia Frost approval.

**Seller position:** Release addressed post-Completion, undated and without undertaking or approval mechanism.

**Analysis:** Without an irrevocable undertaking pre-Release or Release conditions, seller could default or delay release after Completion funds arrive. That creates a gap where Riverlank debt remains outstanding despite the sale price allocation.

**Push back:** Model the Riverlank release exactly to your playbook:

- Release commences upon Completion of funds.
- Require irrevocable undertaking by seller.
- Irrevocable undertaking valid until Release or Amelia Frost approval exception.
- Include a cashflow waterfall confirming direct repayment from Completion funds, not intercompany timing.

Treat absence of these as voidable.

---

## 9. Employee Bonuses DD-005 — AUD 420,000
**Playbook:** Must be a specific line item or seller-funded; funds flow must not silently exclude it.

**Seller position:** Not separately itemised in completion funds flow; no separate designation; taxed and on-costs status unspecified.

**Analysis:** While disclosure acknowledges the AUD 420,000 amount exists, the SPA draft does not reflect the cash outlay. Silent omission invites buyer claims that promised bonuses were not drawn down and that on-costs or payroll tax remain undisclosed.

**Push back:** Reframe DD-005 into a specific SPA line item labelled “Employee completion bonuses AUD 420,000 (completion conditions)” and include it in the completion funds flow. State whether payroll tax, superannuation and employer on-costs apply per Schedule per pay item and quantify amounts if quantified. That preserves the agreed transferability regime and prevents misleading omission.

---

## 10. Ironquay IP — AUD 180,000
**Playbook:** Broaden the narrow indemnity, preserving the SOW3 cure; the AUD 180,000 is not independently verified either way.

**Seller position:** Existing indemnity limited to SOW3 payment; considered adequate.

**Analysis:** The seller flatly rejects broadening. Yet the disclosure admits DD-010 shows AUD 180,000 open with no receipt of payment, no independent bank verification, and no confirmatory assignment. On that basis the seller cannot demonstrate the listed amount has been paid or serviced, which creates a simple and enforceable deficiency claim under the indemnity rather than against the broad cap.

**Push back:** Update Clause 11.1 to broaden the Ironquay indemnity to cover unascertained IP losses attributable to the SOW3 matter up to the total SOW3 amount, with provision for cure within a reasonable period following execution of SOW3 amounts. Add an express indemnity obligation for failure to pay, assign or provide certifications. Keep the SOW3 cure intact but remove the “adequate” characterisation.

---

## 11. Export / Privacy Incident DD-006
**Playbook:** Preserve logs, investigate, require updates; assume no confirmed breach, harm, notification duty or numeric demand in either direction.

**Seller position:** Download link provided; ~1,240 records; preliminary; not confirmed breach; no harm amount stated; no investigation disclosed as ongoing.

**Analysis:** The seller treats this as low-materiality. But “preliminary” and “no confirmed breach” leave open the possibility that:

- An unauthorised access occurred.
- Notification obligation existed.
- Privacy impact arises under Australian law (Privacy Act regime).
- Potential regulatory liability could attach regardless of whether confirmed breach.

Closing an oversight incident risks buyer unawareness.

**Push back:** Explicitly preserve logs, open an investigation now with interim findings, and require DD-006 periodic disclosure for 12 months post-Completion regardless of materiality characterisation. Preserve buyer enforcement rights.

---

## 12. Sandbar Renewals — AUD 330,000
**Playbook:** Assess; no automatic Debt classification or price deduction.

**Seller position:** Ordinary course operating costs.

**Analysis:** The seller’s pro-forma classification suppresses scrutiny. Each renewal is AUD 110,000 in DD-008/DD-011, three instances recorded together, with timing and unavoidable characteristics unclear. If they fall outside ordinary course, they could be significant supplier obligations post-acquisition. That is a commercial fact worth quantification, but the seller does not explain why each renewal meets every “ordinary course” definition, nor does it document specificity.

**Push back:** Request separate documentation for each renewal, specifying dates, amounts, and basis. Decide classification by application of strict ordinary-course test with supporting documentation. Preserve right to reclassify if grounds emerge. No automatic deduction risk without genuine support. Keep separate from debt mechanics; if any amount moves to wider category, reflect back to seller explicitly.

---

## 13. Title Claim Source Evidence
**Playbook:** Independent title/ownership/encumbrance/authority evidence; DD-012 register is supplied internal source, not independent proof.

**Seller position:** Share register at DD-012 identifies Harbourglass Ventures as holder of 100%.

**Analysis:** A corporate register entry is merely the seller’s historical record; it does not satisfy the “independent” criterion. Buyers commonly need external verification: statutory filings, share registers from a different registrar, third-party holdings-verification letters, court records or liens searches. Relying solely on DD-012 without independent corroboration would be buyer-concessionary and risky in view of potential encumbrances not yet recorded.

**Push back:** Require independent corroborating evidence: outside statutory extract, third-party registration verification, lien searches or reference to buyer’s own confirmatory enquiries executed pre-signing. Document the analysis showing title free of fictitious shares, liens, or qualifications. Retain DD-012 as supporting evidence only.

---

## 14. Buyer Knowledge Exclusions (Clause 8.3)
**Playbook:** Delete blanket buyer-knowledge exclusions; any qualifier needs named seller knowledge persons + reasonable enquiry; never excuse title, capacity, fraud or specific indemnity.

**Seller position:** General disclosure from data room and public records; clauses 8.3-ish.

**Analysis:** The seller keeps a blanket exclusion capturing everything discoverable from data room or public records. That is a blunt instrument: it suppresses information critical to assessing title, capacity, underlying fraud and IP claims, potentially clawing out our core negotiating positions. A specific, narrow qualifier would better protect both parties.

**Push back:** Delete or narrow the blanket clause to discrete, enumerable scenarios: buyer’s own searches that have materially failed to turn up facts already disclosed. Avoid capturing situations where seller had inadequate access or no enquiry. Named parties only. Retain a deletion of any undefined “buyer knowledge” without defined qualifier. Never excuse title, capacity, fraud or specific indemnity claims.

---

## Summary Table

| Issue | Playbook Standard | Seller Draft | Action |
|---|---|---|---|
| General warranty cap | 25% / AUD 6,000,000 (conditional 20% authority required) | 20% / AUD 4,800,000 unconditional | Push back to 25% or add conditional override requirement with documentation |
| Thresholds | AUD 5,000 / AUD 50,000 | AUD 25,000 / AUD 250,000 | Revert to playbook values |
| Time limit | 24 months general; 18 months fallback with Amelia authority | 18 months broad | Restore 24 months; optional 18 months only with enhanced documentation |
| Title/capacity regime | Separate, 100% cap, ≥6 years | Merged into general regime | Restore independent category |
| Fraud carve-out | Required maximum, non-waivable | Absent | Insert and bullet-point |
| Disclosure | Specific fair disclosure, case-by-case | General data-room reliance | Require specific exhibits, preserve buyer rights |
| Bluefen consent | Pre-Completion effective consent + conditions evidence | Deemed satisfied on delivery | Insert condition precedent |
| Riverlank release | Repayment + irrevocable undertaking + Amelia approval | Undated post-Completion release | Restructure release mechanism |
| DD-005 bonuses | Specific line item, funded | Silent omission | Insert line item in SPA and funds flow |
| Ironquay IP | Broader indemnity with SOW3 cure preserved | Limited to SOW3 payment, “adequate” | Expand coverage; delete adequacy characterisation |
| DD-006 Export | Open-ended preservation and investigation | Preliminary, low materiality | Add ongoing disclosure obligation; preserve logs |
| DD-008 Sandbar renewals | Strict assessment, no automatic debt | “Ordinary course” generic | Request per-renewal documentation; clarify classification |
| DD-010/DD-012 Title | Independent title

**Seller position:** Not separately itemised in completion funds flow; no separate designation; taxed and on-costs status unspecified.

**Analysis:** While disclosure acknowledges the AUD 420,000 amount exists, the SPA draft does not reflect the cash outlay. Silent omission invites buyer claims that promised bonuses were not drawn down and that on-costs or payroll tax remain undisclosed.

**Push back:** Reframe DD-005 into a specific SPA line item labelled “Employee completion bonuses AUD 420,000 (completion conditions)” and include it in the completion funds flow. State whether payroll tax, superannuation and employer on-costs apply per Schedule per pay item and quantify amounts if quantified. That preserves the agreed transferability regime and prevents misleading omission.

## 10. Ironquay IP — AUD 180,000
**Playbook:** Broaden the narrow indemnity, preserving the SOW3 cure; the AUD 180,000 is not independently verified either way.

**Seller position:** Existing indemnity limited to SOW3 payment; considered adequate.

**Analysis:** The seller flatly rejects broadening. Yet the disclosure admits DD-010 shows AUD 180,000 open with no receipt of payment, no independent bank verification, and no confirmatory assignment. On that basis the seller cannot demonstrate the listed amount has been paid or serviced, which creates a simple and enforceable deficiency claim under the indemnity rather than against the broad cap.

**Push back:** Update Clause 11.1 to broaden the Ironquay indemnity to cover unascertained IP losses attributable to the SOW3 matter up to the total SOW3 amount, with provision for cure within a reasonable period following execution of SOW3 amounts. Add an express indemnity obligation for failure to pay, assign or provide certifications. Keep the SOW3 cure intact but remove the “adequate” characterisation.

## 11. Export / Privacy Incident DD-006
**Playbook:** Preserve logs, investigate, require updates; assume no confirmed breach, harm, notification duty or numeric demand in either direction.

**Seller position:** Download link provided; ~1,240 records; preliminary; not confirmed breach; no harm amount stated; no investigation disclosed as ongoing.

**Analysis:** The seller treats this as low-materiality. But “preliminary” and “no confirmed breach” leave open the possibility that:

- An unauthorised access occurred.
- Notification obligation existed.
- Privacy impact arises under Australian law (Privacy Act regime).
- Potential regulatory liability could attach regardless of whether confirmed breach.

Closing an oversight incident risks buyer unawareness.

**Push back:** Explicitly preserve logs, open an investigation now with interim findings, and require DD-006 periodic disclosure for 12 months post-Completion regardless of materiality characterisation. Preserve buyer enforcement rights.

## 12. Sandbar Renewals — AUD 330,000
**Playbook:** Assess; no automatic Debt classification or price deduction.

**Seller position:** Ordinary course operating costs.

**Analysis:** The seller’s pro-forma classification suppresses scrutiny. Each renewal is AUD 110,000 in DD-008/DD-011, three instances recorded together, with timing and unavoidable characteristics unclear. If they fall outside ordinary course, they could be significant supplier obligations post-acquisition. That is a commercial fact worth quantification, but the seller does not explain why each renewal meets every “ordinary course” definition, nor does it document specificity.

**Push back:** Request separate documentation for each renewal, specifying dates, amounts, and basis. Decide classification by application of strict ordinary-course test with supporting documentation. Preserve right to reclassify if grounds emerge. No automatic deduction risk without genuine support. Keep separate from debt mechanics; if any amount moves to wider category, reflect back to seller explicitly.

## 13. Title Claim Source Evidence
**Playbook:** Independent title/ownership/encumbrance/authority evidence; DD-012 register is supplied internal source, not independent proof.

**Seller position:** Share register at DD-012 identifies Harbourglass Ventures as holder of 100%.

**Analysis:** A corporate register entry is merely the seller’s historical record; it does not satisfy the “independent” criterion. Buyers commonly need external verification: statutory filings, share registers from a different registrar, third-party holdings-verification letters, court records or liens searches. Relying solely on DD-012 without independent corroboration would be buyer-concessionary and risky in view of potential encumbrances not yet recorded.

**Push back:** Require independent corroborating evidence: outside statutory extract, third-party registration verification, lien searches or reference to buyer’s own confirmatory enquiries executed pre-signing. Document the analysis showing title free of fictitious shares, liens, or qualifications. Retain DD-012 as supporting evidence only.

## 14. Buyer Knowledge Exclusions (Clause 8.3)
**Playbook:** Delete blanket buyer-knowledge exclusions; any qualifier needs named seller knowledge persons + reasonable enquiry; never excuse title, capacity, fraud or specific indemnity.

**Seller position:** General disclosure from data room and public records; clauses 8.3-ish.

**Analysis:** The seller keeps a blanket exclusion capturing everything discoverable from data room or public records. That is a blunt instrument: it suppresses information critical to assessing title, capacity, underlying fraud and IP claims, potentially clawing out our core negotiating positions. A specific, narrow qualifier would better protect both parties.

**Push back:** Delete or narrow the blanket clause to discrete, enumerable scenarios: buyer’s own searches that have materially failed to turn up facts already disclosed. Avoid capturing situations where seller had inadequate access or no enquiry. Named parties only. Retain a deletion of any undefined “buyer knowledge” without defined qualifier. Never excuse title, capacity, fraud or specific indemnity claims.
